column2: Ashamed, though knowing dharma, he did not tell his nephew, the great-souled Parvata, of his keen desire.
Then Parvata understood it from his austerity and signs, and, angry at Narada afflicted by desire, cursed him greatly:

You made an agreement with me, calmly, that whatever resolve there is in the heart, good or bad,

Understanding his words, Narada in anger then cursed his nephew Parvata, the uncle his nephew:
Though you are joined with austerity, celibacy, truth and self-control, and ever devoted to dharma, you shall not obtain a dwelling in heaven.
Having cursed each other, greatly enraged and intolerant, the two went each his way like two angry best of elephants.
Parvata, the great sage, roamed the whole earth, honoured as is just by his own splendour, Bharata.
Then Narada, best of the righteous, rightly obtained that maiden, Srinjaya's daughter, the tender, blameless one.
But the maiden, as by the curse, saw Narada as a monkey from the very time of the hand-taking mantras.
The tender maiden, seeing the divine sage with a monkey-like face, did not scorn him then but was pleased.
She attended her husband and did not go to another even in thought, god, sage or Yaksha, devoted to her husband as a wife.
Then once the revered Parvata came searching and in a secluded forest he saw Narada.
Saluting him, Parvata then said to Narada: "Lord, show me favour by granting me a place in heaven."
Seeing Parvata sitting with joined palms, wretched, Narada, himself more wretched, said to him:

You first cursed me, 'You will be a monkey'; and I afterwards, so told, cursed you too from resentment: 'From today you will not obtain a dwelling in heaven.'

Then, seeing Narada, prosperous and of divine form, the tender maiden, suspecting him a stranger, ran away.
Seeing her blameless running, Parvata said: "This is your husband; there is no need for doubt.
The sage, supremely righteous, the revered lord Narada, is your very own; do not doubt this."
Pacified in many ways by the great-souled Parvata, hearing of her husband's curse-fault, she returned to her own nature; Parvata then went to heaven and Narada went home.
This great sage Narada was an eyewitness to everything; asked, he will tell you what happened, best of men."

[Yudhishthira said:] "I do not doubt your word, ascetic, what you say; for dharma is evident to you, best of upholders of all dharma.
Men appointed by the Lord do good and bad deeds, O king; the fruit of the deed goes to the Lord.
As a man who fells a tree in the forest with an axe, the sin would be the feller's, never the axe's.
Or if, by taking it up, they would obtain the fruit of the deed, the sin made by rod and weapon does not exist in the man.
It is not accepted, son of Kunti, that the fruit made by another should be obtained; therefore place it on the Lord.
Or if man is the doer of good and bad deeds, there is nothing beyond; therefore do another good.
No one, O king, ever turns back from what is fated; the sin made by rod and weapon does not exist in the man.
Or if you think the world is established on chance, even so no evil deed has been or will be.
Or if the world's approach to good and bad is to be taken, the raising of the rod is the most approached by kings.
Even so, in the world deeds revolve, Bharata, and I think they bring the fruit of good or bad.
Thus the truth, the good teaching, the fruit of the deed is certain; give it up, tiger among kings; do not set your mind on grief.
For one abiding in his own dharma, even if blameworthy, Bharata, such self-abandonment is not fitting for you, O king.
Expiations are prescribed here for doers of deeds, son of Kunti; one with a body can perform them, one without a body would be undone.
So, O king, while living you will perform the expiation; but having not performed expiation, you will be tormented after death, Bharata."

[Vyasa said:] "One who does not do the prescribed rite, practises the forbidden, and lives falsely, is subject to expiation.
One for whom the sun has risen while he was a celibate student, or has set, one with defective nails or black teeth,
the younger brother married before the elder, the elder unmarried, a Brahmana who has forsaken the Veda, a slanderer, the husband of a woman previously married, and the first such woman,
one who breaks his vow of celibacy, a slayer of the twice-born, one who gives up a Brahmana at a wrong place, and one who does not give at a tirtha,
a village priest, son of Kunti, a seller of a king, a slayer of a Shudra or a woman—each earlier is the more blameworthy.
One who vainly slaughters animals, a forest-burner, one who serves by lies, and one who obstructs his teacher,
one who casts away the sacred fires, a seller of the Veda—these are all sins, and he who has broken an agreement.
I shall also tell the things that are not to be done; hear them from me, those that conflict with the world and the Veda; listen with a single mind.
One who being capable does not perform the rites beginning with the installation of fires, and, Bharata, does not give all that is always to be given,
non-giving of fees, and touching a Brahmana: those who know dharma call all these things not to be done.
A son who divides with his father, and one who defiles his teacher's bed; a man who does not beget offspring is unrighteous by adharma.
These deeds have been told in detail and briefly, for doing or not doing which a person becomes subject to expiation.
But hear in which circumstances men doing these very deeds are not stained.
One who kills, in battle, a man even versed in the Vedanta who comes against him with weapon raised and wishing to slay him is not a slayer of a Brahmana.
On this too, son of Kunti, a mantra is recited in the Vedas; I tell you that dharma prescribed by the authority of the Veda.
One who kills a Brahmana fallen from his conduct, an attacker, is not a slayer of a Brahmana; anger meets anger.
One who, when life is at stake or from ignorance, drinks wine, if unprompted and devoted to dharma, deserves a rite of purification again.
All this has been told to you, son of Kunti, about eating the forbidden; all is purified by the rule of expiation.
Intercourse with a teacher's bed for the teacher's purpose does not defile a man; Uddalaka begot Shvetaketu through a pupil.
In calamities, one who commits theft for his teacher's sake is not bound, unless he acts so often by desire.
One who takes from those who are not Brahmanas is not defiled; and one who has not eaten himself is not stained by sin.
To save a life, untruth may be spoken for oneself or another, for a teacher's sake, with women, and in marriages.
A vow is not broken by seminal emission in a dream in any way; a ghee oblation in a kindled fire is prescribed as the expiation.
Marrying before an elder brother is not a fault when the brother is fallen or has gone forth, nor intercourse with another's wife who begs; that does not stain dharma.
One should neither make vain slaughter of animals nor have it done; kindness to animals is the rite enjoined by the rule.
A gift given to an unworthy Brahmana in ignorance is not a fault; so also giving at a tirtha or elsewhere, for a reason.
For unchaste women there is a purification which is not defiling; she too is purified by it, but the husband is not defiled.
Knowing the truth, the sale of soma is not defiling; dismissing a servant who is unable is blameless; burning a forest for the sake of cattle is not defiling.
These deeds have been told which one does without being defiled; I shall tell the expiations in detail, Bharata."
